title: Lactating cow feeding practices on a dairy farm

lessons.title: Feeding systems on South African dairies
lessons.html:
Learning the farm's feeding system

In this work experience module you will take part in the daily feeding of lactating cows on a real dairy and record your tasks in your logbook. First learn which system your farm uses.

SystemWhere it is commonHow cows are fed
Pasture-basedCoastal areas of the Western and Eastern Cape, KZN MidlandsGrazing kikuyu, ryegrass and clover, with meal in the parlour
Total mixed ration (TMR)Inland, drier areas such as the Free State and North WestCows housed or in feedlot-style pens, fed a mixed ration from a mixer wagon
Mixed (partial TMR)Many areasGrazing plus a mixed ration on a feed pad

Feeding groups

Cows are grouped so each group gets the right ration. Typical groups:

  • Fresh cows: recently calved, watched closely.
  • High producers: most energy and protein.
  • Low producers / late lactation: less concentrate to avoid getting fat.
  • Heifers in first lactation: sometimes kept separate, as they are still growing and get bullied.

Moving cows between groups is decided by the manager using yield and stage of lactation. Record every move so the parlour feeder and feed sheet stay correct.

The feeding day

  1. Check the feed sheet and any changes.
  2. Clean troughs and remove refusals; record the amount.
  3. Mix and deliver feed, or allocate fresh pasture, after each milking.
  4. Push up feed during the day.
  5. Check water points and fences.
  6. Record feed fed and observations.

Spend your first days watching an experienced feeder. Learn where each feed is stored, how the mixer wagon scale works, which camp each group grazes and how refusals are measured. Ask questions and write the answers in your logbook.

lessons.title: Feeding through the lactation
lessons.html:
The transition period

The three weeks before and after calving are the most risky time in a cow's life. Her feed intake drops just as milk demand rises fast. Most metabolic diseases happen now.

  • Close-up dry cows get a special ration set by the nutritionist to prepare the rumen and help prevent milk fever.
  • Fresh cows get the best roughage and a gradual build-up of concentrates.
  • Watch fresh cows daily: appetite, rumen fill, dung, temperature and milk yield.

Problems linked to feeding

ProblemFeeding linkSigns
AcidosisToo much starch, too little fibre, sudden ration changesLoose dung, low cud chewing, lameness, low milk fat
BloatLush clover or lucerne, hungry cows on new pastureSwollen left side, distress. Emergency
KetosisToo little energy in early lactation, fat cows at calvingOff feed, drop in milk, sweet smell on breath
Milk feverCalcium balance around calvingWobbly, down, cold ears

Call the supervisor and vet straight away for bloat, milk fever and down cows.

Body condition scoring

Body condition score (BCS) shows fat cover on a scale, commonly 1 (very thin) to 5 (very fat). Look at the backbone, ribs, hip and pin bones and tail head. Cows should calve in moderate condition, lose some in early lactation, and regain it slowly in mid and late lactation. Score cows regularly and record the scores; big losses after calving point to underfeeding or illness.

Water

Check troughs at every visit. Cows drink most just after milking, so water near the parlour exit is important. Clean troughs weekly or more often in summer.

lessons.title: Measuring and improving feeding results
lessons.html:
Using information to check feeding

A good feeder keeps an eye on numbers and on the cows themselves.

Records to use

  • Milk recording: yields per cow and per group, butterfat and protein. A fall in butterfat can show too little fibre; very low protein can show too little energy.
  • Feed records: kilograms fed per group and refusals. These let the manager work out feed cost per litre.
  • Feed stock: silage, hay and meal on hand, so the manager can order before running out.

Simple calculation

If a group of 100 cows is fed 1 800 kg of meal in a day and produces 2 600 litres, the meal per litre is 1 800 ÷ 2 600 = about 0.69 kg meal per litre. At R6.50 per kg of meal, meal cost is about R4.50 per litre. Your manager compares this with the milk price to see if feeding is profitable.

Looking at the cows

  • Rumen fill: a sunken hollow on the left side behind the ribs means the cow has not eaten enough.
  • Cud chewing: most resting cows should be chewing.
  • Dung: should stack slightly, not run or form hard balls. Undigested grain or long fibres show digestion problems.
  • Sorting: cows that dig out meal and leave long roughage need the mix or chop length checked.

Reducing waste

  • Keep silage covered and the face tidy.
  • Store meal dry and off the floor, controlling rats and birds.
  • Avoid spilling feed when loading.
  • Feed to appetite, not far above it.

Key points

  • Know your farm's feeding system and the groups of cows.
  • The transition period around calving needs the closest attention.
  • Acidosis, bloat, ketosis and milk fever are linked to feeding; report signs quickly.
  • Score body condition and use milk recording to check feeding.
  • Record feed fed and refusals so cost per litre can be worked out.
